newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North Koreans make history with boat escape.
newsitem.headline: North Koreans make history with boat escape.

text.p: Two North Korean families staged a daring escape by boat to the South on Monday in what was thought to be the first defection of its kind from the hunger-stricken communist nation.
The group of 14 people, including a two year-old child, was one of the largest ever to flee the impoverished nation, authorities in the western port of Inchon said.

Their wooden vessel, disguised as a Chinese fishing trawler, was intercepted off the west coast of the Korean peninsula just south of a military demarcation line that has split the two Koreas since their 1950-53 war.
"If the information provided by the captain is true, it would be the first defection direct by sea from North Korea," said Korea Maritime Police spokesman Chung Moo-chung.
Captain Ahn Sun-kook, 48, his wife, mother, son and two daughters formed one family. The other was led by the boat's engineer and included his two year-old grandson.
They had outwitting North Korean naval patrol craft before being spotted by Southern naval radar.
The group abandoned their 32 tonne boat on a South Korean island and boarded a navy ship for the voyage to Inchon, where they were expected early on Tuesday.

Chronic food shortages are driving growing numbers of desperate citizens to flee North Korea, risking their lives in search of rice and a better life. In recent weeks several have walked across the heavily-mined land border.
The largest mass escape was by a group of 17 -- including 16 members of a single family -- that arrived in the South last December after a six-week long epic escape through China.
Last month North Korea's former top ideologue, Hwang Jang-yop, arrived in Seoul after a flight through Beijing and the Philippines.
Meanwhile, a U.N. aid official reported that famine was ticking away like a timebomb in the country.
World Food Programme (WFP) official Tun Myat told a news conference in Beijing there was a "famine in slow motion".
"It's ticking away like a time bomb," said Myat, a Burmese, who is in charge of WFP transport and logistics.

Babies and children were afflicted in varying degrees by malnutrition and hospitals were bare of equipment and patients because people could not afford to send sick relatives for treatment, Myat said.
"They ate bark and leaves," he said, referring to people he saw during a two-week visit.

"Stalks of corn, cobs of corn, empty pea and bean pods, mushroom stems and whatever that in most other countries would either have been thrown away or would have at best been used for animal feed are now being milled into powder."
In some areas seaweed had become a major staple, and it was difficult to say when the "point of no return" would come.
The WFP estimates North Korea urgently needs 1.3 million tonnes of food. It has appealed for 200,000 tonnes worth $96 million, but has received only $38 million to date.
Separately, South Korea's Red Cross said it would begin delivering 15,000 tonnes of corn to the North next week and seek the resumption of talks with its Northern counterpart.
Secretary General Lee Byung-woong said his organisation planned to give its North Korean counterpart an estimate of how much other food aid was planned.

That issue had created a deadlock in inter-Korean Red Cross talks in Beijing aimed at speeding up shipments. The talks, held earlier this month, were the first contact between the two Korean organisations in nearly five years.
The North demanded to know the exact amount of aid before discussing delivery.
South Korea wants all shipments to be sent directly over the land border, instead of by ship through the International Committee of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.
